{{Short description|Abelian group with no non-trivial torsion elements}}
{{Group theory sidebar}}

In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[abstract algebra]], a '''torsion-free abelian group''' is an [[abelian group]] which has no non-trivial [[torsion (algebra)|torsion]] elements; that is, a [[group (mathematics)|group]] in which the [[group operation]] is [[commutative property|commutative]] and the [[identity element]] is the only element with finite [[order (group theory)|order]]. 

While [[finitely generated abelian group]]s are completely classified, not much is known about infinitely generated abelian groups, even in the torsion-free countable case.<ref>See for instance the introduction to {{Citation | last=Thomas | first= Simon | title=The classification problem for torsion-free abelian groups of finite rank | zbl=1021.03043 | journal=J. Am. Math. Soc. | volume=16 | issue=1 | pages=233–258 | year=2003| doi= 10.1090/S0894-0347-02-00409-5 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Definitions ==
{{main|Abelian group}}

An [[abelian group]] <math> \langle G, + ,0\rangle </math> is said to be torsion-free if no element other than the identity <math> e </math> is of finite [[Order of a group element|order]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Fraleigh|1976|p=78}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Lang|2002|p=42}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Hungerford|1974|p=78}}</ref> Explicitly, for any <math>n > 0</math>, the only element <math>x \in G</math> for which <math>nx = 0</math> is <math>x = 0</math>. 

A natural example of a torsion-free group is <math> \langle \mathbb Z,+,0\rangle </math>, as only the integer 0 can be added to itself finitely many times to reach 0. More generally, the [[free abelian group]] <math>\mathbb Z^r</math> is torsion-free for any <math>r \in \mathbb N</math>. An important step in the proof of the classification of finitely generated abelian groups is that every such torsion-free group is isomorphic to a <math>\mathbb Z^r</math>. 

A non-finitely generated countable example is given by the additive group of the polynomial ring <math>\mathbb Z[X]</math> (the free abelian group of countable rank). 

More complicated examples are the additive group of the rational field <math>\mathbb Q</math>, or its subgroups such as <math>\mathbb Z[p^{-1}]</math> (rational numbers whose denominator is a power of <math>p</math>). Yet more involved examples are given by [[Rank of an abelian group#Groups_of_higher_rank|groups of higher rank]].

==Groups of rank 1==

===Rank===
{{ Main | Rank of an abelian group }}
The ''rank'' of an abelian group <math>A</math> is the dimension of the <math>\mathbb Q</math>-vector space <math>\mathbb Q \otimes_{\mathbb Z} A</math>. Equivalently it is the maximal cardinality of a linearly independent (over <math>\Z</math>) subset of <math>A</math>. 

If <math>A</math> is torsion-free then it injects into <math>\mathbb Q \otimes_{\mathbb Z} A</math>. Thus, torsion-free abelian groups of rank 1 are exactly subgroups of the additive group <math>\mathbb Q</math>.

===Classification===
Torsion-free abelian groups of rank 1 have been completely classified. To do so one associates to a group <math>A</math> a subset <math>\tau(A)</math> of the prime numbers, as follows: pick any <math>x \in A \setminus \{0\}</math>, for a prime <math>p</math> we say that <math>p \in \tau(A)</math> if and only if <math>x \in p^kA</math> for every <math>k \in \mathbb N</math>. This does not depend on the choice of <math>x</math> since for another <math>y \in A\setminus \{0\}</math> there exists <math>n, m \in \mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}</math> such that <math>ny = mx</math>. Baer proved<ref>{{cite journal | author=Reinhold Baer | authorlink=Reinhold Baer | title=Abelian groups without elements of finite order | journal=[[Duke Mathematical Journal]] | volume=3 | year=1937 | issue=1 | pages=68–122 | doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-37-00308-9 | url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/duke-mathematical-journal/volume-3/issue-1/Abelian-groups-without-elements-of-finite-order/10.1215/S0012-7094-37-00308-9.short| url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | author=Phillip A. Griffith | title=Infinite Abelian group theory | series=Chicago Lectures in Mathematics | publisher=University of Chicago Press | year=1970 | isbn=0-226-30870-7 }} Chapter VII.</ref> that <math>\tau(A)</math> is a complete isomorphism invariant for rank-1 torsion free abelian groups.

==Classification problem in general==
The hardness of a classification problem for a certain type of structures on a countable set can be quantified using [[model theory]] and [[descriptive set theory]]. In this sense it has been proved that the classification problem for countable torsion-free abelian groups is as hard as possible.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Paolini |first1=Gianluca |last2=Shelah |first2=Saharon |eprint=2102.12371 |title=Torsion-Free Abelian Groups are Borel Complete |class=math.LO |date=2021}}</ref>
